original_question: Let X be a smooth projective variety, let B be a line bundle on X, and let L_d be a sufficiently positive line bundle. Theorem 4.11 shows that p-jet very ampleness of B implies K_{p,1}(X,B;L_d) = 0 for d sufficiently large, while the existence of a reduced zero-cycle of length p + 1 that fails to impose independent conditions on H^0(X,B) implies K_{p,1}(X,B;L_d) != 0 for d sufficiently large. What are the necessary and sufficient conditions on B and X for the vanishing of K_{p,1}(X,B;L_d) when d is sufficiently large?
target_in_paper: Problem 4.12 in Section 4, posed immediately after Definition 4.10 and Theorem 4.11 as the higher-dimensional extension of the curve result Theorem 4.3.
correct_elements: The draft correctly identifies the Section 4 weight-one syzygy problem, accurately paraphrases the two partial results in Theorem 4.11, and asks for a characterization of when K_{p,1}(X,B;L_d) vanishes asymptotically. That is exactly the open problem formalized in the paper as Problem 4.12.
missing_details: The paper works over the complex numbers: X is a smooth complex projective variety.
The problem is meant in the standing notation of Section 1: choose an ample line bundle/divisor A and an arbitrary line bundle/divisor P, and set L_d = dA + P.
One must require d to be large enough that L_d is very ample and defines the embedding used to form the Koszul cohomology groups.
The integer p should be fixed in advance and is independent of d.

K_{p,1}(X,B;L_d) should be defined as the weight-1 Koszul cohomology group coming from the minimal graded free resolution over S = Sym H^0(X,L_d) of the graded module R(X,B;L_d) = ⊕_m H^0(X, B + mL_d).
The quantifier d >> 0 should be made explicit as: there exists an integer d_0 such that the asserted vanishing holds for all integers d >= d_0.
The intended unresolved scope is the higher-dimensional case dim X >= 2; the curve case is already completely answered by Theorem 4.3.

The exact definition of p-jet very ampleness should be stated if referenced: for every effective zero-cycle w = a_1x_1 + ... + a_sx_s of degree p+1, the map H^0(X,B) -> H^0(X, B ⊗ O_X / m_w) is surjective, where m_w = m_{x_1}^{a_1} ... m_{x_s}^{a_s}.
The exact obstruction used in Theorem 4.11 should be spelled out if referenced: there exists a reduced zero-cycle w = x_1 + ... + x_{p+1} such that H^0(X,B) -> H^0(X, B ⊗ O_w) is not surjective.
A stand-alone formulation should not blur the paper's distinction between p-very ampleness and p-jet very ampleness in higher dimensions.
refined_question: Fix an integer p >= 0. Let X be a smooth complex projective variety of dimension n >= 2, let A be an ample line bundle and P an arbitrary line bundle on X, and set L_d = dA + P, with d sufficiently large so that L_d is very ample. For a line bundle B on X, let K_{p,1}(X,B;L_d) denote the weight-one Koszul cohomology group of the graded S-module R(X,B;L_d) = ⊕_m H^0(X, B + mL_d), where S = Sym H^0(X,L_d). Find necessary and sufficient geometric conditions on the pair (X,B), relative to p, such that there exists d_0 with K_{p,1}(X,B;L_d) = 0 for every integer d >= d_0.
justification: The draft is not targeting the introductory asymptotic nonvanishing statements of Section 1; it paraphrases Theorem 4.11 and then asks exactly the follow-up open problem stated immediately afterward as Problem 4.12. The surrounding Section 4 context shows that this is meant as the unresolved higher-dimensional analogue of Theorem 4.3 for curves, where asymptotic vanishing is already characterized by p-very ampleness. To make the question fully stand-alone and faithful to the paper, one must import the standing notation from Section 1 for L_d and for the Koszul cohomology groups K_{p,q}(X,B;L_d), make the asymptotic quantifier explicit, and note that the paper is specifically discussing the dim X >= 2 case here. The remark after Problem 4.12 also explains why the paper does not simply replace the question by p-very ampleness: p-jet very ampleness is known to suffice, but p-very ampleness is treated as doubtful in higher dimension.
